title: The gravitational field equations
one_line_summary: Builds Einstein's field equation by pairing a recap of curvature (Riemann, Ricci tensor, Ricci scalar) with a field-theory rewrite of Newtonian gravity whose Poisson equation serves as template, refutes the tempting guess Ricci = kappa T using the contracted Bianchi identity and energy-momentum conservation, repairs it with the divergence-free Einstein tensor, fixes kappa = 8 pi G / c^4 from the Newtonian limit, and then derives the trace-reversed form and the cosmological-constant form.
role_in_book: This is the payoff chapter of Part II. Chapter 6 argued that gravity must be a field theory of the metric obeying some differential equation; Chapters 7-10 supplied the covariant derivative, geodesics, connection coefficients and measurement frames; Chapter 11 built the Riemann and Ricci tensors; Chapter 12 built the energy-momentum tensor and its conservation law. Chapter 13 joins the geometric and physical threads into G = 8 pi G T - Lambda g, closes Part II with a checklist of working heuristics, and hands the equation to Chapter 14 (survey of triumphs), Part III (cosmology, where Lambda returns) and Part IV (Schwarzschild solutions). The plausibility-style derivation is later deepened in Part V: the Bianchi identity is treated in Chapter 43, an action-based motivation appears in Chapter 40, and the Newtonian limit is redone in Chapter 45.

learning_objectives: Reader can describe the schematic statement (curvature of spacetime) = (energy density of matter) and name which tensor fills each side and why.
Reader can trace the chain metric -> connection coefficients -> Riemann tensor -> Ricci tensor -> Ricci scalar and say that curvature needs up to second derivatives of the metric.
Reader can derive the gravitational Poisson equation from Newton's integral expression for the field using the delta-function identity for the Laplacian of 1/|x - x'|.
Reader can identify -1/|x - x'| as the Green's function of the Laplacian (with the 4 pi normalization) and use it to write the potential of an arbitrary mass distribution.
Reader can explain the Newtonian template 'two derivatives of the potential proportional to the source' and why it suggests 'two derivatives of g proportional to T'.
Reader can list three ways Einstein's gravity must differ from Newton's: no instantaneous action, light deflection by gravity, and nonlinearity because energy both sources and responds to geometry.
Reader can state local causality, local energy-momentum conservation, the dominant energy condition and the weaker energy condition as requirements on the source.
Reader can contract the Bianchi identity to 2 R^alpha_{gamma;alpha} = R_{;gamma} and use it with metric compatibility to prove the Einstein tensor is divergence-free.
Reader can show that the candidate equation R^{mu nu} = kappa T^{mu nu} plus div T = 0 forces the trace of T to be the same everywhere, and explain why that rules the candidate out.
Reader can reduce the 00 component of G = kappa T in the weak-field, low-pressure limit to Poisson's equation and deduce kappa = 8 pi G / c^4 (about 2.08e-43 N^-1).
Reader can trace the field equation to get R = -8 pi G T and rewrite it in trace-reversed form R_{mu nu} = 8 pi G (T_{mu nu} - g_{mu nu} T / 2).
Reader can justify why a term -Lambda g may be added without spoiling conservation, and recast it as a vacuum energy-momentum tensor T^vac = -Lambda g / (8 pi G).
Reader can explain why, unlike electromagnetism, general relativity does not let one fix the source first and then solve for the field.

teaching_approach.summary: A short synthesis chapter that runs two tracks in parallel, geometry and physics, and makes them meet (Fig. 13.1). The physics track rewrites Newton's gravity as a field theory so that Poisson's equation becomes the pattern to imitate; the geometry track is a compressed recap of Chapter 11. The decisive pedagogical choice is to put a plausible but wrong field equation on the table and let a conservation-law consistency check destroy it, so the Einstein tensor enters as the repair rather than as an unexplained formula. The constant is fixed by demanding the Newtonian limit, the equation is displayed in three boxed 'versions', and the chapter closes with a bulleted toolkit of habits for the application chapters. Index manipulations are fenced into Example boxes, with a margin note restating the physics for readers who find them distracting.
narrative_arc: Goal stated as a word equation: curvature on the left, energy density of matter on the right; a two-column route map (Fig. 13.1) shows geometry and physics converging on G = 8 pi G T.

Geometry recap: the metric is a classical field; coordinate choices can fake acceleration, so the Riemann tensor is needed to isolate genuine curvature; Riemann in terms of Gamma, then Ricci tensor and Ricci scalar.
Correspondence principle: any relativistic theory must reduce to Newton, so Newton is rewritten as a field theory: force law, potential, integral field law.
Example 13.1 turns the integral law into Poisson's equation via the delta-function identity; Example 13.2 recasts the same result with a Green's function.
Template extracted: replace potential by metric and mass density by energy density to get the schematic boxed equation (two derivatives of g) = kappa T.
Caveats: Newton is instantaneous, light bends, and in GR the source itself depends on the metric, so the theory must be nonlinear (Fig. 13.2).
Requirements on the source: local causality, local conservation of energy-momentum, dominant energy condition; all packaged in T with div T = 0.
Tempting guess R^{mu nu} = kappa T^{mu nu} because both sides are rank-2; take its divergence and ask what happens on the geometric side.
Example 13.3 introduces the Bianchi identity (boundary of a boundary) and contracts it; the Einstein tensor is defined and shown to be divergence-free.
Collision: the guess plus the contracted Bianchi identity forces the Ricci scalar, hence the trace of T, to be constant everywhere; a lumpy universe contradicts this, so the guess is dropped.
Repair: adopt G_{mu nu} = kappa T_{mu nu}, whose divergence vanishes identically on both sides.
Example 13.4 fixes kappa by the weak-field, dust-dominated limit, temporarily restoring c: kappa = 8 pi G / c^4, with its SI value.

Boxed version 1 (G = 8 pi G T); Example 13.5 traces it to get version 2 (trace-reversed Ricci form); adding -Lambda g gives version 3, reinterpreted as vacuum energy-momentum, with a pointer to Part III.
Closing toolkit of heuristics (light cones, two kinds of frame, index rules, general covariance, perfect-fluid components) and a three-bullet chapter summary.
signature_moves: Propose-and-refute: a natural candidate equation is written down explicitly (labelled 'incorrect guess') and killed by a consistency test, so the correct equation arrives as the fix.
Conservation as the selection principle: the physics requirement div T = 0 must be matched by a geometric identity, which singles out the trace-reversed Ricci tensor.
Newtonian field theory recast as a template with a boxed schematic equation (box of second derivatives of g equals box of kappa T) before any tensor detail.
Constant of proportionality left undetermined until the end and then fixed by correspondence with Poisson's equation, with factors of c reinstated just for that calculation.
Three numbered, boxed 'versions' of the same field equation, signalling equivalent forms and the one permissible extra term.
Margin 'physics recap' for readers who find the index algebra distracting, restating the logic of the Bianchi argument in words.
Geometry-versus-physics two-column route diagram that organizes the whole chapter.
End-of-part checklist of practical heuristics that consolidates Part II habits before applications.

sections.title: Chapter opening: the target equation and the route
sections.summary: States the central idea of general relativity as a word equation linking spacetime curvature to the energy density of matter, announces that this chapter finally supplies both sides, and lays out the route in Fig. 13.1: shared physical principles branch into a geometry column (metric to curvature to G) and a physics column (matter fields to energy to 8 pi G T) that meet in the field equation.

sections.title: Geometry: a recap of the key ingredients
sections.summary: Recalls that the metric is a classical tensor field expressed through the line element. Because a single particle's acceleration could be a coordinate artefact, genuine gravity must be detected by removing coordinate effects, which is what the Riemann tensor does; it is obtained from the relative acceleration of initially parallel free particles and written in terms of connection coefficients (first derivatives of g) and their derivatives. Two contractions, the symmetric Ricci tensor and the Ricci scalar, are flagged as the ingredients of the left-hand side. A margin note suggests that the (1,3) Riemann tensor is the best candidate for 'the gravitational field', but its valence does not match the (2,0) energy-momentum tensor.

sections.title: Physics: the key ingredients
sections.summary: Imposes the principle that a relativistic theory must reproduce Newton in the non-relativistic limit and therefore rewrites Newtonian gravity as a field theory: force law, potential energy, potential per unit mass, then integral expressions for the field and potential of a continuous density. Example 13.1 shows the field is minus the gradient of the potential and, using the delta-function divergence identity, derives Poisson's equation; Example 13.2 re-expresses the solution with the Green's function -1/|x - x'|. The pattern (two derivatives of a potential proportional to a source) is transplanted into the schematic relativistic guess of second derivatives of g proportional to kappa T. The section then lists the differences from Newton (instantaneous action, bending of light, nonlinearity because T depends on g, Fig. 13.2) and the physical requirements on the source: local causality, local conservation of energy-momentum, and the dominant energy condition, all carried by an energy-momentum tensor obeying div T = 0.

sections.title: An incorrect guess
sections.summary: Because T has two indices, the natural guess is to equate it to the Ricci tensor, R^{mu nu} = kappa T^{mu nu}, which was Einstein's own first attempt in autumn 1915. Taking the divergence kills the right side by conservation. Example 13.3 introduces the Bianchi identity (motivated by 'the boundary of a boundary is zero', like div curl = 0), contracts it twice to obtain 2 R^alpha_{gamma;alpha} = R_{;gamma}, and the Einstein tensor G^{mu nu} = R^{mu nu} - g^{mu nu} R / 2 is defined and shown divergence-free using metric compatibility. Combining this with the guess forces the gradient of the Ricci scalar to vanish; the guess then makes the trace of T a universal constant, which is incompatible with a clumpy universe, so the candidate is abandoned.

sections.title: Einstein's field equation
sections.summary: The object uncovered while refuting the guess becomes the solution: G_{mu nu} = kappa T_{mu nu} has zero divergence on both sides. Example 13.4 fixes kappa in the weak-field limit: with nearly Minkowski metric and T dominated by T^00 = rho c^2, the spatial Einstein components vanish, giving R = 2 R^00 and G^00 = 2 R_00 = (2/c^2) Laplacian Phi, so matching Poisson yields kappa = 8 pi G / c^4. The field equation is boxed as version 1; Example 13.5 traces it (R = -8 pi G T) to give the trace-reversed version 2. Admitting that the route was a plausibility argument, the section adds -Lambda g (allowed because the metric is covariantly constant) to get version 3, interprets Lambda as an extra energy source that repels when positive, and rewrites it as a vacuum energy-momentum tensor, deferring its history to Part III.

concepts.name: Einstein field equation
aliases: version 1 of the Einstein field equation
concepts.definition: The tensor field equation of general relativity relating geometry to matter: the Einstein tensor built from the metric and its first two derivatives equals 8 pi G / c^4 times the energy-momentum tensor (optionally minus Lambda times the metric). It is ten coupled nonlinear second-order partial differential equations for the metric components.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached as the repair of a failed candidate: after R^{mu nu} = kappa T^{mu nu} is shown to force a uniform trace of T, the divergence-free Einstein tensor replaces the Ricci tensor, and the constant is fixed by matching Poisson's equation. Displayed in three boxed versions (plain, trace-reversed, with Lambda).
concepts.notes: Book uses c = 1 but keeps G explicit in this chapter; later chapters set G = 1.

concepts.name: Einstein tensor
concepts.definition: The symmetric rank-2 tensor G_{mu nu} = R_{mu nu} - (1/2) g_{mu nu} R formed from the Ricci tensor and scalar; by the contracted Bianchi identity its covariant divergence vanishes identically for any metric. Its trace is -R, so it is the Ricci tensor with its trace reversed.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined inside the refutation of the Ricci guess, as the combination whose divergence is forced to zero by the contracted Bianchi identity; then promoted to the left-hand side of the correct equation.
concepts.notes: Bold G for the tensor collides with Newton's constant G (margin note 17) and with the Green's function G(x, x') of Example 13.2.

concepts.name: Ricci-tensor field equation (rejected candidate)
concepts.definition: The proposal that the Ricci tensor itself is proportional to the energy-momentum tensor. Combined with energy-momentum conservation and the contracted Bianchi identity it forces the Ricci scalar, and hence the trace of T, to be constant throughout spacetime, which contradicts the observed non-uniform distribution of matter.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the obvious rank-2 match for T, credited in a margin note to Einstein's first attempt in 1915, then refuted by taking the divergence of both sides.

concepts.name: Bianchi identity
concepts.definition: The differential identity satisfied by the Riemann tensor of any metric-compatible, torsion-free connection: the cyclic sum of its covariant derivatives over the last three lower-index positions vanishes, R^a_{b[cd;e]} = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted without proof in Example 13.3 and motivated by the slogan that the boundary of a boundary is zero, the same idea behind div curl = 0; full treatment deferred to Chapter 43.

concepts.name: contracted Bianchi identity
concepts.definition: The result of contracting the Bianchi identity twice: twice the divergence of the mixed Ricci tensor equals the gradient of the Ricci scalar, 2 R^alpha_{gamma;alpha} = R_{;gamma}, equivalently the Einstein tensor is divergence-free.
concepts.how_introduced: Worked out step by step in Example 13.3 by setting alpha = lambda, using Riemann antisymmetries, then raising beta and contracting with delta.
concepts.notes: Geometric counterpart of energy-momentum conservation; this match is the logical heart of the chapter.

concepts.name: local conservation of energy-momentum
concepts.definition: The requirement that energy and momentum of matter fields obey a local continuity equation, expressed covariantly as T^{mu nu}_{;mu} = 0, so that nothing is created or destroyed at a point.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed among the physical principles the source must satisfy, identified with the constraint div T = 0 from Chapter 12, and then used as the test that eliminates the Ricci guess and selects the Einstein tensor.
concepts.notes: The text says T encodes conservation 'at least approximately'; in curved spacetime the covariant law is exact but does not give a globally conserved total energy.

concepts.name: Einstein gravitational coupling constant
concepts.definition: The proportionality constant between the Einstein tensor and the energy-momentum tensor, kappa = 8 pi G / c^4, about 2.08e-43 N^-1 in SI units, reducing to 8 pi G when c = 1.
concepts.how_introduced: Left as an unknown kappa through the argument and fixed in Example 13.4 by requiring the 00 component to reproduce Poisson's equation.
prerequisites: Newtonian limit of the field equation
concepts.notes: Its tiny size is why enormous energy densities are needed for appreciable curvature.

concepts.name: Newtonian limit of the field equation
concepts.definition: The approximation of nearly flat spacetime (metric close to Minkowski), static fields and non-relativistic matter with pressure negligible compared with rho c^2, in which the 00 component of the Einstein equation reduces to Poisson's equation for the Newtonian potential.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried out in Example 13.4 with c restored: vanishing spatial Einstein components give R = 2 R^00, and R_00 is identified with the Laplacian of Phi over c^2.
concepts.notes: Treated again with linearized theory in Chapter 45 and surveyed in Chapter 14.

concepts.name: correspondence with Newtonian gravity
concepts.definition: The requirement that a relativistic, geometric theory of gravity reproduce Newton's law of gravitation in the regime of weak fields and slow motion.
concepts.how_introduced: Opens the physics section as the guiding principle, motivating a field-theory rewrite of Newton and, later, the determination of kappa.

concepts.name: Riemann curvature tensor
concepts.definition: The (1,3) tensor built from connection coefficients and their first derivatives (hence from first and second derivatives of the metric) that vanishes everywhere if and only if spacetime is flat; it governs the relative acceleration of nearby free-falling particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Recapped as the tool that strips out coordinate artefacts to reveal genuine curvature, extracted from the geodesic deviation equation; a margin note calls it the best candidate for the gravitational field while noting its valence does not fit the field equation directly.

concepts.name: Ricci tensor
concepts.definition: The symmetric rank-2 tensor obtained by contracting the upper index of the Riemann tensor with its third index, R_{mu nu} = R^alpha_{mu alpha nu}; physically it captures the part of curvature that changes the volume of a small ball of free particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Recapped as the first contraction of Riemann; its symmetry is flagged for later use; margin notes describe it as an average of Riemann that makes volumes shrink.

concepts.name: Ricci scalar
concepts.definition: The full trace of the Ricci tensor with the metric, R = g_{mu nu} R^{mu nu}, a coordinate-invariant scalar field.
concepts.how_introduced: Recapped as the second contraction; later shown to be constant under the rejected guess and equal to -8 pi G T under the correct equation.

concepts.name: metric tensor field
concepts.definition: A symmetric (0,2) tensor defined at every spacetime point that determines intervals via ds^2 = g_{mu nu} dx^mu dx^nu; in GR it is the dynamical field whose equation of motion is the Einstein equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a classical field (point in, tensor out) and as the relativistic replacement for the Newtonian potential in the Poisson template.

concepts.name: connection coefficients
concepts.definition: Coefficients describing how basis vectors change from point to point; for the Levi-Civita connection they are fixed by first derivatives of the metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in a margin formula as the convenient intermediate through which Riemann is usually written.

concepts.name: geodesic deviation
concepts.definition: The relative covariant acceleration of two neighbouring free-fall world lines, which is proportional to the Riemann tensor contracted with the four-velocity and separation.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled as the operational route by which the Riemann tensor was extracted in Chapter 11.
concepts.notes: Margin eqn 13.4 prints this without the minus sign; Chapter 11 is itself inconsistent (11.38 without, 11.6 and 11.39 with). The minus-sign form is the one consistent with the book's Riemann convention.

concepts.name: coordinate acceleration versus curvature
concepts.definition: The observation that one particle's apparent acceleration can arise from a poor coordinate choice or a homogeneous field, so gravity is only unambiguously identified through coordinate-independent curvature, detectable via relative motion of several particles.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in 13.1 to motivate why the Riemann tensor, rather than the metric or connection, belongs in the field equation.

concepts.name: tensor valence matching
concepts.definition: A tensor equation can only equate objects of the same type (same numbers of upper and lower slots); this constrains which curvature object can equal T.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 5 explains that the (1,3) Riemann tensor cannot be set equal to the (2,0) T; the Ricci guess is chosen because it has two indices.

concepts.name: Newtonian gravitational field
concepts.definition: The vector field giving gravitational force per unit test mass at each point, g(x) = -G integral of rho(x') (x - x') / |x - x'|^3 over sources, equal to minus the gradient of the potential.
concepts.how_introduced: Generalized from the two-body force law to a continuous density as the first step of recasting Newton as a field theory.
formulas: \vec g(\vec x) = -G\int\mathrm{d}^3x'\,\rho(\vec x')\frac{\vec x - \vec x'}{|\vec x - \vec x'|^3}
concepts.notes: Arrowed g is the Newtonian field, not the bold metric g.

concepts.name: Newtonian gravitational potential
concepts.definition: The scalar field Phi(x) = -G integral of rho(x') / |x - x'| d^3x', the gravitational potential energy per unit test mass, whose negative gradient is the gravitational field.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by dividing the potential energy U by the test mass, then generalized to a density; it plays the role later taken by the metric.

concepts.name: Laplacian of 1/r identity
concepts.definition: The distributional result that the Laplacian of 1/|x - x'| equals -4 pi delta^(3)(x - x'), equivalently the divergence of (x - x')/|x - x'|^3 is 4 pi delta^(3)(x - x').
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted in Example 13.1 to convert the integral field law into a differential one; proof assigned as Exercise 13.2 via second derivatives of 1/r and Gauss's theorem.

concepts.name: Poisson's equation for gravity
concepts.definition: The Newtonian field equation Laplacian Phi = 4 pi G rho: two spatial derivatives of the potential are proportional to the mass density; in empty regions it reduces to Laplace's equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in Example 13.1 by taking the divergence of the integral field law, then used as the structural template and as the limit that fixes kappa.

concepts.name: Green's function
concepts.definition: For a linear differential operator L, a function G(x, y) satisfying L G = delta(x - y); the solution for a general source is the superposition A(x) = integral of G(x, y) f(y) dy.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 11 gives the general idea; Example 13.2 identifies -1/|x - x'| (with 4 pi normalization) as the Green's function for gravitational Poisson.
concepts.notes: Superposition works only because Newtonian gravity is linear, which is exactly what fails in GR.

concepts.name: nonlinearity of general relativity
concepts.definition: The property that the field equation is not linear in the metric: the source T depends on the metric being solved for, and gravitational energy itself acts back on the geometry, so solutions cannot simply be superposed.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued from the loop in Fig. 13.2 (source fixes geometry, geometry shapes source) and contrasted in margin note 13 with electromagnetism and Newtonian gravity, where sources can be fixed first.

concepts.name: local causality
concepts.definition: A signal can pass between two events only if their separation is timelike or null, never spacelike; fields and sources must respect the light-cone structure.
concepts.how_introduced: First of the physical principles constraining the right-hand side, also used to fault Newton's instantaneous action.

concepts.name: dominant energy condition
concepts.definition: The requirement that every observer measures a non-negative local energy density and a causal (timelike or null) energy flux, so positive energy never flows faster than light.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed as the third principle on the source; later invoked (loosely) to explain why a positive Lambda acts with opposite sign to ordinary matter.

concepts.name: weak energy condition
concepts.definition: The less restrictive requirement that the energy density measured by every observer be non-negative, with no condition on the energy flux.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in margin note 14 as a looser alternative to the dominant energy condition.

concepts.name: energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: The symmetric rank-2 tensor field whose components give energy density, momentum density or energy flux, and stresses of all non-gravitational fields; it vanishes only where all matter fields vanish and it sources gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 12 as the single object carrying causality, positivity and conservation requirements; its T^00 = rho c^2 dominance is used in the Newtonian limit.

concepts.name: trace of the energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: The scalar T = g^{mu nu} T_{mu nu}; for a perfect fluid with signature (-,+,+,+) it equals -rho + 3p (c = 1), vanishing for radiation.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears twice: as the quantity the Ricci guess would force to be constant, and in Example 13.5 where tracing the correct equation gives R = -8 pi G T.
concepts.notes: Perfect-fluid trace formula is the standard result, not printed in this chapter.

concepts.name: trace-reversed form of the Einstein equation
aliases: version 2 of the Einstein field equation
concepts.definition: The equivalent form R_{mu nu} = 8 pi G (T_{mu nu} - (1/2) g_{mu nu} T), obtained by tracing the field equation to find R = -8 pi G T and substituting back; in vacuum it reduces to R_{mu nu} = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in Example 13.5 using g^{mu nu} g_{mu nu} = 4 in four dimensions.
concepts.notes: The vacuum consequence R_{mu nu} = 0 is not stated in this chapter but is what Schwarzschild solves.

concepts.name: cosmological constant
aliases: version 3 of the Einstein field equation
concepts.definition: A constant Lambda multiplying the metric that may be added to the field equation, G_{mu nu} + Lambda g_{mu nu} = 8 pi G T_{mu nu}, without spoiling conservation because the metric has zero covariant derivative; a positive value produces cosmic repulsion.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced after admitting the derivation was haphazard and asking which extra terms are permitted; interpreted as an additional energy source and its Einstein history deferred to Part III.
concepts.notes: The repulsion comes from the negative pressure p = -rho of the vacuum term, not from a negative energy density; see gaps.

concepts.name: vacuum energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: The effective source T^vac = -Lambda g / (8 pi G) that reproduces the cosmological-constant term when moved to the right-hand side; it describes a medium with energy density Lambda / (8 pi G) and pressure equal to minus that density.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as a bookkeeping device to keep the compact form G = 8 pi G (T^mat + T^vac).
concepts.notes: Density and pressure expressions are standard consequences with signature (-,+,+,+), not printed here.

concepts.name: metric compatibility of the connection
concepts.definition: The property of the Levi-Civita connection that the covariant derivative of the metric vanishes, so the metric (and its inverse) can be moved through covariant derivatives freely.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked in margin note 18 when differentiating the Einstein tensor, and again to show the Lambda g term has zero divergence.

concepts.name: covariant derivative of a scalar field
concepts.definition: For a scalar field the covariant derivative reduces to the ordinary partial derivative, f_{;mu} = f_{,mu}, since there are no components to transport.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 20, used to read R^{;nu} = 0 as the statement that R is constant.

concepts.name: symmetries of the Riemann tensor
concepts.definition: The fully lowered Riemann tensor changes sign when the first two or the last two indices are swapped, and is symmetric under exchange of the two pairs.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited in margin note 16 to justify the contraction steps of the Bianchi identity.

concepts.name: boundary of a boundary is zero
concepts.definition: The topological fact that the boundary of any region has no boundary itself; in calculus it appears as div curl = 0 and curl grad = 0, and in geometry it underlies the Bianchi identity.
concepts.how_introduced: Used only as a one-line motivation for the Bianchi identity in Example 13.3.
concepts.notes: Developed properly with chains and Stokes' theorem in Part V.

concepts.name: general covariance
concepts.definition: The principle that a valid tensor equation of special relativity remains valid in curved spacetime once the Minkowski metric is replaced by g and partial derivatives by covariant derivatives.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed in the closing heuristics as the practical recipe for upgrading flat-space physics.

concepts.name: coordinate frame versus orthonormal frame
concepts.definition: Coordinate bases are convenient for geometric calculation and use g to move indices; orthonormal frames represent what observers measure and use eta, though their connection coefficients are generally non-zero unless the frame is locally inertial.
concepts.how_introduced: Closing heuristics list.

concepts.name: light cones as a picture of the metric
concepts.definition: Visualizing a metric by drawing at each event the set of null directions solving ds^2 = 0, which shows causal structure and how it tilts or narrows in curved spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: First bullet of the closing heuristics.

concepts.name: perfect fluid energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: The energy-momentum tensor of a fluid with no viscosity or heat flow, diagonal in its rest frame with energy density rho and isotropic pressure p.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in the closing heuristics with its components in an orthonormal spherical-polar frame.

key_equations.name: Word form of Einstein's equation
key_equations.meaning: Schematic target of the chapter: geometry on the left determined by matter energy on the right.

key_equations.name: Line element
key_equations.meaning: Components of the metric field expressed through the interval between neighbouring events.
key_equations.symbols: g_{mu nu}: metric components; dx^mu: coordinate displacements

key_equations.name: Connection coefficients from the metric
key_equations.latex: \Gamma^{\mu}_{\alpha\beta} = \frac12 g^{\mu\lambda}\left(\frac{\partial g_{\lambda\alpha}}{\partial x^\beta} + \frac{\partial g_{\lambda\beta}}{\partial x^\alpha} - \frac{\partial g_{\alpha\beta}}{\partial x^\lambda}\right)
key_equations.meaning: Margin recap: Gamma is built from first derivatives of g.

key_equations.name: Geodesic deviation (sign restored)
key_equations.meaning: Relative acceleration of neighbouring free particles is fed by the Riemann tensor. The margin note prints it with no minus sign, matching GA eqn 11.38, but GA eqns 11.6 and 11.39 carry the minus (the component form is D^2 xi^a/dtau^2 = -R^a_{bcd} u^b xi^c u^d), so the Chapter 11 sign is restored here.
key_equations.symbols: xi: separation vector; u: 4-velocity of the fiducial geodesic; D/dtau: covariant derivative along it

key_equations.name: Riemann tensor components
key_equations.meaning: Curvature at each event from Gamma and its first derivatives, i.e. from up to second derivatives of g.
key_equations.symbols: alpha output index; beta transported vector; gamma, delta plane of the loop

key_equations.name: Ricci tensor
key_equations.meaning: Contract the upper Riemann index with the third slot; the result is symmetric.

key_equations.name: Ricci scalar
key_equations.meaning: Full trace of the Ricci tensor, a coordinate-invariant scalar.

key_equations.name: Newton's law of gravitation
key_equations.meaning: Attractive inverse-square force on m due to M at displacement r.
key_equations.symbols: G = 6.672(4)e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 as quoted

key_equations.name: Gravitational potential energy
key_equations.meaning: Scalar potential energy whose negative gradient is the force; dividing by m gives the potential Phi.

key_equations.name: Field of a continuous mass distribution
key_equations.latex: \vec g(\vec x) = -G\int\mathrm{d}^3x'\,\rho(\vec x')\frac{\vec x - \vec x'}{|\vec x - \vec x'|^3}
key_equations.meaning: Superposition of inverse-square contributions from every mass element.
key_equations.symbols: rho: mass density; g: force per unit mass

key_equations.name: Potential of a continuous mass distribution
key_equations.meaning: Scalar potential built by superposition.

key_equations.name: Gradient of inverse distance
key_equations.latex: \vec\nabla_{\vec x}\left(\frac{1}{|\vec x - \vec x'|}\right) = -\frac{\vec x - \vec x'}{|\vec x - \vec x'|^3}
key_equations.meaning: Direct computation linking the field integrand to the potential integrand.

key_equations.name: Field as gradient of potential
key_equations.latex: \vec g(\vec x) = \vec\nabla_{\vec x}\int\mathrm{d}^3x'\,\frac{G\rho(\vec x')}{|\vec x - \vec x'|} = -\vec\nabla\Phi(\vec x)
key_equations.meaning: Part (i) of Example 13.1: the integral field law follows from the potential.

key_equations.name: Laplacian of inverse distance
key_equations.meaning: Point-source identity; proof is Exercise 13.2.

key_equations.name: Divergence of the inverse-square kernel
key_equations.latex: \vec\nabla_{\vec x}\cdot\left(\frac{\vec x - \vec x'}{|\vec x - \vec x'|^3}\right) = 4\pi\delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x')
key_equations.meaning: Equivalent form of 13.14 used to take the divergence of 13.10.

key_equations.name: Divergence of the Newtonian field
key_equations.latex: \vec\nabla\cdot\vec g(\vec x) = -4\pi G\int\mathrm{d}^3x'\,\rho(\vec x')\delta^{(3)}(\vec x - \vec x') = -4\pi G\rho(\vec x)
key_equations.meaning: The delta function collapses the integral to the local density. (The printed line drops the arrow on g.)

key_equations.name: Poisson's equation (derived)
key_equations.meaning: Combining 13.16 with g = -grad Phi.

key_equations.name: Newtonian field equation in terms of g
key_equations.meaning: Local Gauss law: mass density is the source (sink) of field lines.

key_equations.name: Poisson's equation (boxed)
key_equations.meaning: Two derivatives of the potential equal a constant times the source density; the structural template for Einstein's equation and the limit that fixes kappa.

key_equations.name: Green's function solution recipe
key_equations.latex: \hat L G(x,y) = \delta(x-y)\ \Rightarrow\ A(x) = \int\mathrm{d}y\,G(x,y)f(y)\ \text{solves}\ \hat L A = f
key_equations.meaning: General superposition principle for linear equations (margin note 11).

key_equations.name: Defining equation of the gravitational Green's function
key_equations.meaning: Normalization with 4 pi chosen to match the form of Poisson's equation (differs from note 11's convention).
key_equations.symbols: G(x, x'): Green's function, not Newton's constant

key_equations.name: Potential from the Green's function
key_equations.meaning: Superpose point-source responses; the prefactor G is Newton's constant, the integrand G is the Green's function.

key_equations.name: Green's function for the Laplacian
key_equations.meaning: Read off by comparison with 13.11 and 13.14.

key_equations.name: Schematic relativistic template
key_equations.meaning: Postulate by analogy with Poisson: second derivatives of the metric proportional to the energy-momentum tensor.

key_equations.name: Incorrect guess
key_equations.meaning: Tempting rank-2 match of Ricci to energy-momentum; shown to be untenable.

key_equations.name: Divergence of the incorrect guess
key_equations.meaning: The right side vanishes by conservation, so the left side must too.

key_equations.name: Energy-momentum conservation
key_equations.meaning: Local conservation law the field equation must respect.

key_equations.name: Bianchi identity
key_equations.meaning: Cyclic identity on covariant derivatives of Riemann; the geometric counterpart of a conservation law.

key_equations.name: Bianchi identity contracted once
key_equations.meaning: Set alpha = lambda and use Riemann antisymmetry to recognize Ricci tensors.

key_equations.name: Contracted Bianchi identity
key_equations.meaning: Raise beta and contract with delta: twice the divergence of Ricci equals the gradient of the Ricci scalar.

key_equations.name: Einstein tensor
key_equations.meaning: Trace-reversed Ricci tensor.
key_equations.symbols: bold G: Einstein tensor, distinct from Newton's G

key_equations.name: Divergence of the Einstein tensor
key_equations.meaning: Metric compatibility lets g pass through the covariant derivative.

key_equations.name: Applying the contracted Bianchi identity
key_equations.meaning: Raising and renaming dummy indices shows the two terms cancel.

key_equations.name: Einstein tensor is divergence-free
key_equations.meaning: An identity true for every metric, matching the conservation law of T.

key_equations.name: Consequence of the incorrect guess
key_equations.meaning: If Ricci is divergence-free (guess plus conservation) then div G = 0 forces the Ricci scalar to be constant.

key_equations.name: Constant trace contradiction
key_equations.meaning: The guess would require the trace of T to be the same everywhere, i.e. a uniform universe, so it is rejected.

key_equations.name: New candidate field equation
key_equations.meaning: Both sides are divergence-free identically, so consistency with conservation is automatic.

key_equations.name: Spatial Einstein components in the Newtonian limit
key_equations.meaning: With pressure and momentum flux negligible, the spatial source components vanish.

key_equations.name: Sum of spatial Ricci components
key_equations.meaning: Each diagonal spatial Ricci component equals R/2.

key_equations.name: Ricci scalar in the Newtonian limit
key_equations.meaning: Intermediate step of Example 13.4.

key_equations.name: 00 Einstein component in the Newtonian limit
key_equations.meaning: Uses g^{00} ~ -1 so that G^00 = R^00 + R/2.

key_equations.name: Weak-field connection and curvature
key_equations.latex: \Gamma^i_{00} = \frac{\partial(\Phi/c^2)}{\partial x^i},\qquad R^i{}_{0j0} = \frac{\partial^2(\Phi/c^2)}{\partial x^i\partial x^j},\qquad R_{00} = \sum_i R^i{}_{0i0}
key_equations.meaning: Recalled weak-field results: curvature components are the Newtonian tidal tensor; tracing gives the Laplacian.

key_equations.name: Einstein 00 component as Laplacian of the potential
key_equations.meaning: Links the geometric side to Newtonian gravity.

key_equations.name: Predicted Newtonian field equation
key_equations.meaning: What G = kappa T gives with T^00 = rho c^2.

key_equations.name: Coupling constant
key_equations.meaning: Matching 13.41 to Poisson's equation.

key_equations.name: Einstein field equation, version 1 (components)
key_equations.meaning: The field equation of general relativity (c = 1).

key_equations.name: Einstein field equation, version 1 (index-free)
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate-free statement at each event.

key_equations.name: Trace of the field equation
key_equations.meaning: Contract with the inverse metric.

key_equations.name: Ricci scalar from the trace of T
key_equations.meaning: Curvature scalar fixed algebraically by the local trace of energy-momentum.

key_equations.name: Einstein field equation, version 3 (components)
key_equations.meaning: Most general form allowed by the divergence argument, with cosmological constant Lambda.

key_equations.meaning: Coordinate-free version with Lambda.

key_equations.name: Lambda absorbed into the source

key_equations.name: Vacuum energy-momentum tensor
key_equations.meaning: Effective source equivalent to the cosmological constant; with signature (-,+,+,+) it has rho = Lambda/(8 pi G) and p = -rho.

key_equations.meaning: Statement to be proved in Exercise 13.2.

figures.label: Fig. 13.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Road map to Einstein's equation: the geometric branch ends in the Einstein tensor, which is built from Riemann curvature, and the physical branch ends in 8 pi G times the energy-momentum tensor.
figures.visual_description: Two tall grey vertical bands side by side, headed 'Geometry' on the left and 'Physics' on the right in bold. A small white box labelled 'PRINCIPLES' straddles the gap near the top; two white arrows fan out from it, one down-left into the geometry band and one down-right into the physics band. The left band then reads, top to bottom and joined by white downward arrows, 'Metric' then 'Curvature' in italics, ending in a large bold G at the bottom. The right band reads 'Matter fields' then 'Energy', ending in a large bold T preceded by 8 pi G. An equals sign sits in the gap between the two bottom symbols, so the bottom row reads G = 8 pi G T across both bands.
figures.what_it_teaches: The field equation is a meeting of two independent chains of reasoning, one geometric and one physical, rooted in shared principles; each side must be constructed before they can be equated.

redesign.idea: Living route map whose nodes unfold into the actual mathematics: the geometry chain expands g -> Gamma -> Riemann -> Ricci/R -> G, the physics chain expands matter fields -> T with its conservation law and energy conditions, and the equals sign only 'locks' once both sides are shown divergence-free.
redesign.interaction: Learner clicks a node to reveal its defining equation, a one-line meaning and a mini-demo (e.g. Riemann opens a geodesic-deviation animation, T opens a dust/fluid component table). A 'check divergence' button on each side animates the Bianchi identity and div T = 0; if the learner swaps G for the Ricci tensor, the lock fails and a warning explains the constant-trace contradiction.

figures.label: Fig. 13.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Feedback loop in Einstein's theory: the energy-momentum source, constrained by conservation, shapes the metric field and hence geometry, while the metric in turn fixes the form of the source.
figures.visual_description: Two stacked rectangles with dashed inner borders: the upper one labelled 'source' in bold, the lower one labelled 'fields'. A thick curved outline arrow on the left runs from the upper box down to the lower box, with the words 'conservation laws' written vertically beside it. A matching curved arrow on the right runs from the lower box back up to the upper box, labelled 'geometry' written vertically. Together the arrows form a closed clockwise-looking cycle between source and fields.
figures.what_it_teaches: In general relativity source and field cannot be specified in sequence: matter tells geometry how to curve (subject to conservation), and geometry determines how matter's energy-momentum is expressed and moves, making the theory nonlinear and self-consistent rather than a one-way source-to-field map.

redesign.idea: Side-by-side 'one-way versus loop' solver. Left panel: electromagnetism or Newtonian gravity, where the learner paints a charge or mass density and the field appears in one pass via Green's-function superposition. Right panel: a toy self-gravitating star in which the metric computed from the matter changes the matter's equilibrium profile, which changes the metric again; iterations are shown as the two arrows of the loop lighting up in turn.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets total mass and radius (compactness) with sliders and presses 'iterate'. The app animates successive source/metric passes, plotting density profile and g_tt versus radius at each pass and a convergence meter. At low compactness the loop converges in one or two passes (Newtonian-like, effectively linear); near the compactness limit convergence slows or fails, showing why self-consistency matters.

worked_examples.label: Example 13.1
worked_examples.problem: Starting from the integral expressions for the Newtonian field and potential of a continuous mass density, show that the field is minus the gradient of the potential and derive the differential field equation.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate 1/|x - x'| under the integral to reproduce the inverse-square kernel, giving g = -grad Phi; then take the divergence of the field integral using the identity that the divergence of the kernel is 4 pi times a 3D delta function, collapse the integral, and combine with g = -grad Phi.
worked_examples.key_insight: Action-at-a-distance integrals are equivalent to a local differential equation in which second derivatives of the potential at a point are set by the density at that point, the structural idea carried into GR.
worked_examples.result: div g = -4 pi G rho and Laplacian Phi = 4 pi G rho (eqns 13.16-13.17).

worked_examples.label: Example 13.2
worked_examples.problem: Solve Poisson's equation for gravity by the Green's function method.
worked_examples.method: Define the Green's function as the solution of the Laplacian with a 4 pi delta source, write the potential as G times the integral of the Green's function against the density, and compare with the integral for Phi from Example 13.1 to identify the Green's function.
worked_examples.key_insight: Because the Newtonian equation is linear, the potential of any mass distribution is a superposition of point-source responses; the loss of this superposition property is what makes GR harder.

worked_examples.label: Example 13.3
worked_examples.problem: From the Bianchi identity derive a relation between the divergence of the Ricci tensor and the gradient of the Ricci scalar.
worked_examples.method: Quote the Bianchi identity; contract the upper index with the derivative index, using antisymmetry of Riemann in its index pairs to turn two terms into Ricci tensors; raise the remaining free lower index and contract it with another to obtain Ricci-scalar and Ricci-divergence terms.
worked_examples.key_insight: A purely geometric identity delivers a built-in conservation law for a particular combination of curvature, which is what a field equation sourced by a conserved T needs.
worked_examples.result: 2 R^alpha_{gamma;alpha} = R_{;gamma} (eqn 13.29), the contracted Bianchi identity.

worked_examples.label: Divergence of the Einstein tensor and refutation of the Ricci guess (in-text)
worked_examples.problem: Show that the Einstein tensor is divergence-free and use this to test the candidate equation R^{mu nu} = kappa T^{mu nu}.
worked_examples.method: Take the covariant divergence of R^{mu nu} - g^{mu nu} R/2, pull g through by metric compatibility, substitute the contracted Bianchi identity and rename dummy indices so the terms cancel. Then note the guess plus div T = 0 makes the Ricci divergence zero, so the remaining term forces grad R = 0; tracing the guess converts this into a constant trace of T.
worked_examples.key_insight: The wrong equation fails not through an algebraic error but because it would impose an absurd global restriction on matter; conservation acts as a filter on possible field equations.
worked_examples.result: div G = 0 identically (13.33); the guess would demand g^{mu nu} T_{mu nu} = const everywhere (13.35), so it is rejected.

worked_examples.label: Example 13.4
worked_examples.problem: Find the constant kappa in G_{mu nu} = kappa T_{mu nu} by demanding agreement with Newtonian gravity for weak fields.
worked_examples.method: Take the metric nearly Minkowski so index positions only flip signs on time components; keep only T^00 = rho c^2 since pressure is negligible. Setting spatial Einstein components to zero gives each spatial Ricci diagonal component equal to R/2, hence R = 2R^00 and G^00 = 2R_00. Use the weak-field connection Gamma^i_00 = partial_i Phi / c^2 and the resulting R^i_{0j0} to get R_00 = Laplacian Phi / c^2, then compare G^00 = kappa rho c^2 with Poisson.
worked_examples.key_insight: Only one component of the tensor equation survives in the Newtonian regime, and it is Poisson's equation in disguise; the rest of the tensor structure is invisible to Newton.
worked_examples.result: kappa = 8 pi G / c^4, about 2.08e-43 N^-1; with c = 1, kappa = 8 pi G.
concepts: Newtonian limit of the field equation

worked_examples.label: Example 13.5
worked_examples.problem: Rewrite the Einstein equation so that the Ricci tensor stands alone on the left.
worked_examples.method: Contract the field equation with the inverse metric, use g^{mu nu} g_{mu nu} = 4 to get R - 2R = 8 pi G T, so R = -8 pi G T; substitute into the original equation and rearrange.
worked_examples.key_insight: In four dimensions the curvature scalar is fixed locally by the trace of the source, so the equation can be trace-reversed; the form makes vacuum (Ricci-flat) problems especially transparent.
worked_examples.result: R_{mu nu} = 8 pi G (T_{mu nu} - g_{mu nu} T / 2) (eqn 13.47).
concepts: trace-reversed form of the Einstein equation

worked_examples.label: Cosmological-constant term (in-text)
worked_examples.problem: Determine whether extra terms can be added to G = 8 pi G T without breaking consistency with energy-momentum conservation.
worked_examples.method: Observe that a constant multiple of the metric has zero covariant divergence because g_{mu nu;alpha} = 0, so adding -Lambda g to the right leaves the divergence argument intact; then move the term into an effective source tensor.
worked_examples.key_insight: The consistency argument fixes the equation only up to a term proportional to the metric; that leftover freedom is the cosmological constant.
worked_examples.result: G = 8 pi G T - Lambda g (13.49), equivalently T^vac = -Lambda g / (8 pi G) (13.51).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Poisson's equation as a template: Newtonian potential stands in for the metric, mass density for energy-momentum, and the Laplacian for 'two derivatives'.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Newtonian gravity is rewritten as a local field equation so its shape (second derivatives of a field proportional to a source) can be copied into the schematic relativistic equation with an unknown constant kappa, which is later fixed by the same analogy.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The copy is only structural: GR is nonlinear, the source depends on the metric, and the metric has ten components rather than one potential; the naive rank-2 copy (Ricci = kappa T) actually fails.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Two-row dictionary animation: Phi, rho, Laplacian and 4 pi G morph into g_{mu nu}, T_{mu nu}, second-derivative curvature operator and 8 pi G, with each pair highlighted when the learner hovers over it.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Electromagnetism (and Newtonian gravity) as linear theories where you place the charges first and then solve for the fields.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Margin note 13 contrasts this workflow with GR, where the source tensor is itself expressed with the unknown metric, so metric and matter must be found together.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Maxwell theory in curved spacetime also couples to g; the contrast is about gravity's self-coupling rather than about EM being simpler in every respect.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Paint-a-source sandbox with a 'linear' toggle: in linear mode the field appears immediately by superposition; in GR mode a loop animation shows repeated metric/matter updates.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The Ricci tensor as an average of the Riemann tensor that keeps only the volume-shrinking part of curvature.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Offered in margin notes 15 and 21 to explain why Ricci looked like the natural object to equate to matter and what physical content it carries.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Ricci omits the shape-distorting (Weyl) part, which is exactly what survives in vacuum, so 'average' should not suggest Ricci contains all gravitational effects.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Ball of free test particles falling through a star: display volume change (Ricci) inside the matter and pure shape distortion with constant volume (Weyl) outside.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The boundary of a boundary is zero, as in the vector identity div curl = 0.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: One-sentence motivation that makes an intimidating index identity feel like a familiar vector-calculus fact, deferring the proof to Chapter 43.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only suggestive at this stage; the precise link needs differential forms and the curvature two-form.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Show a cube's faces (boundary) and then the edges of those faces, each edge traversed twice in opposite directions so contributions cancel; link to the analogous cancellation in the Bianchi identity.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A Green's function as the response to a single point source, from which any source's response is built by adding up point responses.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Margin note 11 and Example 13.2 present the solution of Poisson's equation as superposition of -1/|x - x'| kernels.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Superposition is unavailable in full GR; it returns only in linearized theory.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Click to drop point masses on a 2D grid and watch the potential surface add up as a sum of kernels, with a toggle to paint a smooth density.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The Riemann tensor as 'the gravitational field' itself.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Margin note 5 identifies what cannot be transformed away at a point with the physical field of gravitation, while explaining why its valence keeps it off the left side of the field equation.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Riemann corresponds to tidal field (second derivatives of Phi), not to the Newtonian g-vector (first derivative), which is frame-dependent in GR.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Treating the cosmological constant as one more ingredient in the Universe's energy budget.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The Lambda term is moved to the source side as T^vac so the equation keeps its G = 8 pi G T form.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: This 'ingredient' has negative pressure equal in magnitude to its density and does not dilute as space expands, unlike any ordinary matter.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Energy-budget pie with a Lambda slice; toggling Lambda shows T^vac components and the sign of rho + 3p that controls attraction or repulsion.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Two columns, geometry and physics, growing from common principles and meeting at an equals sign.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Fig. 13.1 structures the chapter as building two sides separately before joining them.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The picture hides the feedback of Fig. 13.2: the physics column depends on the metric too.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because the energy-momentum tensor has two indices, the Ricci tensor (also two indices) should simply be set proportional to it.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Rank matching is necessary but not sufficient: the equation must also respect div T = 0. The Ricci tensor is not identically divergence-free, and imposing R^{mu nu} = kappa T^{mu nu} forces a constant trace of T everywhere. The divergence-free Einstein tensor is required.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is the simplest curvature object of the right type, and Einstein himself tried it.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The full Riemann tensor, being the real measure of gravity, should itself appear on the left of the field equation.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Riemann has valence (1,3) while T has valence (2,0); only contractions of Riemann can be equated to T, and the part of Riemann not fixed by matter (the Weyl part) is determined by the field equations plus boundary conditions rather than locally by the source.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Riemann is presented as the definitive, coordinate-independent signature of gravitation.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Since Einstein's equation is modelled on Poisson's equation, one can specify the matter distribution first and then solve for the metric, adding up contributions as in Newtonian gravity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The energy-momentum tensor is built with the metric, and matter moves according to geometry, so source and metric must be solved together; the equations are nonlinear and superposition fails except in the weak-field approximation.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The template analogy and experience with electrostatics and Newtonian potentials.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If a single particle accelerates in some coordinates, gravity (curvature) must be present.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: An accelerating coordinate system or a homogeneous field can mimic the effect; only curvature, revealed by relative acceleration of neighbouring free particles, is an unambiguous signature.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Newtonian physics acceleration relative to coordinates is taken as evidence of a force.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A constant Ricci scalar is by itself what rules out the Ricci guess.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A constant R is not unphysical on its own; the problem arises because the guess ties R to the trace of T, so matter would have to be uniformly spread through the Universe.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The derivation reaches R = const first, which looks like the punchline.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The bold G of the Einstein tensor is the same thing as Newton's gravitational constant G (or the Green's function G).
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Three different objects share the letter in this chapter: the Einstein tensor (rank-2 tensor field), Newton's constant (a number), and the Green's function G(x, x') of Example 13.2.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Identical symbol, often in the same equation (G = 8 pi G T).

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A positive cosmological constant repels because it corresponds to negative energy density.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: With signature (-,+,+,+), T^vac = -Lambda g / (8 pi G) has positive energy density Lambda / (8 pi G) and pressure equal to minus that density; gravitational attraction in GR is sourced by rho + 3p, which is negative here, producing repulsion.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book attributes the repulsion to the opposite sign of the Lambda g term relative to positive T, which readers easily translate into 'negative energy'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Where there is no matter (T = 0), spacetime must be flat.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The trace-reversed form gives R_{mu nu} = 0 in vacuum, which constrains only the Ricci part of curvature; the Riemann tensor can be non-zero (tidal fields around a star, gravitational waves).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Reading 'curvature = energy' literally suggests no energy means no curvature.
concepts: trace-reversed form of the Einstein equation

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The chapter's argument proves Einstein's equation uniquely from first principles.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The authors call their route haphazard: it is a plausibility argument that fixes the equation only once one assumes a linear relation between T and a curvature tensor built from g and its second derivatives, and even then a Lambda g term remains free.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The step-by-step elimination of alternatives feels like a derivation.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Covariant conservation div T = 0 means the total energy of matter in the Universe is conserved, just as in flat spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The covariant law is local; in curved spacetime it cannot generally be integrated into a conserved global total, because matter exchanges energy with the gravitational field, which has no local energy-momentum tensor.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In special relativity the same-looking equation does give global conservation via Gauss's theorem.

thought_experiments.name: Gravity or perverse coordinates?
thought_experiments.setup: Watch a single free particle appear to accelerate in some coordinate system and ask whether a gravitational field is responsible or merely the coordinates.
thought_experiments.lesson: One particle cannot decide; one needs the coordinate-independent residue, curvature, revealed by the changing separation of neighbouring free particles, which motivates the Riemann tensor as the left-side ingredient.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Toggle between a rotating/accelerating grid in flat space and a real tidal field: a lone particle looks the same in both, but a pair of particles reveals the difference.

thought_experiments.name: A universe obeying Ricci = kappa T
thought_experiments.setup: Suppose the Ricci guess were true and apply energy-momentum conservation together with the contracted Bianchi identity, then look at a universe with lumps of matter (e.g. a star surrounded by empty space).
thought_experiments.lesson: The trace of T would have to take the same value inside the star and in the vacuum around it, which is impossible; the guess contradicts the clumpy Universe we see. (The star illustration is the dossier's concrete version of the book's argument.)
thought_experiments.app_idea: Map of trace(T) across a region containing a star; under the Ricci guess a warning overlay shows it must be flat-coloured, while the real equation allows the lump.

thought_experiments.name: Solving for sources and fields in sequence
thought_experiments.setup: Try the electrostatics workflow in GR: write down a star's energy-momentum tensor and then solve for the metric.
thought_experiments.lesson: Writing T already requires the metric (e.g. normalizing four-velocities, lowering indices), so the attempt is circular; one must search for consistent pairs of g and T, which is why GR is hard.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Fig. 13.2 redesign: iterative star solver that lights up each arrow of the loop per iteration.

historical_notes.event: Einstein's first field-equation proposal set the Ricci tensor proportional to the energy-momentum tensor. The book's margin note dates it to October 1915; historians usually tie it to his 4 and 11 November 1915 Academy papers, which came before the final form of 25 November.
historical_notes.significance: Shows that even Einstein went through the tempting rank-2 guess before finding the conservation-consistent form; gives the chapter's refutation a historical anchor.

historical_notes.event: In November 1915 Einstein presented the final field equation with the trace term, after abandoning his first attempt.
historical_notes.significance: Marks the completion of general relativity's field equations.

historical_notes.event: Einstein's introduction of the cosmological constant and later rejection of it, described as physics folklore and deferred to Part III and Chapter 18.
historical_notes.significance: Sets up Lambda's return in cosmology, where it now describes the observed accelerating expansion.

applications_and_observations.topic: Size of the Einstein coupling constant
applications_and_observations.details: In SI units kappa = 8 pi G / c^4 is extraordinarily small, so curvature produced by everyday energy densities is tiny; strong curvature needs astrophysical densities.
Quoted alongside Newton's force law as the constant in the field theory; the value printed is an older determination.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: G = 6.672(4)e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 (book); CODATA 2018 value 6.67430(15)e-11 (dossier note).

applications_and_observations.details: Cited as experimental evidence that gravity cannot simply act within flat space: light, which travels straight in flat spacetime, is deflected, so gravity must warp spacetime.
The everyday fact that matter is clumped (stars, planets, empty space) is the observation that kills the Ricci-tensor guess, which would require a uniform trace of T.

applications_and_observations.topic: Pressure versus energy density in ordinary matter
applications_and_observations.details: The Newtonian limit keeps only T^00 because p is tiny compared with rho c^2. Dossier estimate (not in the book): at the Sun's centre p ~ 2.5e16 Pa and rho c^2 ~ 1.4e22 Pa, a ratio of about 2e-6; in the Earth's core the ratio is of order 1e-10.

Dossier estimate (not in the book): with R = -8 pi G T / c^4 and T ~ -rho c^2 for dust, the Ricci scalar inside rock of mean density 5500 kg/m^3 is about 8 pi G rho / c^2, showing how weakly ordinary matter curves spacetime.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: R ~ 1e-22 m^-2, curvature radius ~ 1e11 m (about 0.7 AU) (own estimate).

notation_and_conventions.convention: (-,+,+,+): in the weak-field limit g_00 ~ g^00 ~ -1 and g_ii ~ g^ii ~ 1.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Hence A^00 ~ A_00 and A^ii ~ A_ii for nearly flat metrics; mixed 0i components flip sign.

notation_and_conventions.convention: c = 1 for most of the chapter with Newton's G kept explicit; factors of c are temporarily restored in Example 13.4; later chapters also set G = 1.
notation_and_conventions.notes: kappa = 8 pi G / c^4 in SI becomes 8 pi G with c = 1.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Bold G is the Einstein tensor, plain G is Newton's constant, and G(x, x') in Example 13.2 is a Green's function.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Margin note 17 flags the first clash; the Green's function clash is not flagged.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Semicolon subscripts denote covariant derivatives, commas partial derivatives; div T is written T^{mu nu}_{;mu}. For scalars the two coincide.

R^alpha_{beta gamma delta} with the derivative of Gamma^alpha_{delta beta} along x^gamma carrying a plus sign (eqn 13.5); Ricci contracts the upper index with the third slot, R_{mu nu} = R^alpha_{mu alpha nu}.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Same as Chapter 11 (MTW-style); with signature (-,+,+,+) this gives G = +8 pi G T.

notation_and_conventions.convention: (m,n) counts upper and lower slots: Riemann is (1,3), the energy-momentum tensor is written as (2,0) with components T^{mu nu}; the Einstein tensor is (2,0) or (0,2).
Lambda appears as -Lambda g on the right-hand side, equivalent to +Lambda g_{mu nu} on the left; positive Lambda is repulsive.
Boxed symbols such as the box of second derivatives of g and the box of kappa T denote the schematic structure of an equation, not precise tensor expressions.
Arrowed symbols (g-vector, F, x) are Euclidean 3-vectors; bold symbols (g, T, R, G) are spacetime tensor fields. delta^(3) is the three-dimensional Dirac delta.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The Newtonian field g-vector and the metric g share a letter.

notation_and_conventions.convention: T^mat and T^vac separate matter and vacuum (Lambda) contributions; hatted indices denote orthonormal-frame components.

margin_notes.summary: Recalls the formula for connection coefficients in terms of first derivatives of the metric.
Restates the geodesic deviation equation used to extract the Riemann tensor, in slot notation; it is printed without the minus sign that GA eqns 11.6 and 11.39 carry (though 11.38 also omits it).
Flags that the Ricci tensor is symmetric, a fact needed later in the chapter.
Reminds the reader that a scalar such as the Ricci scalar takes the same value whatever coordinates it is computed in.

Suggests the Riemann tensor can be regarded as the physical gravitational field despite the equivalence principle, but notes its (1,3) valence prevents inserting it directly opposite the (2,0) energy-momentum tensor.
Points back to Section 0.4 for the earlier Newtonian field discussion, and a later note says the field equation and Poisson equation here repeat eqns 0.12 and 0.15 of the Overture.
Proof hint: compute the gradient of the inverse distance directly; the Laplacian identity with the -4 pi delta function is left to the exercises.
Contrasts Laplace's equation (no sources) with Poisson's equation (sources present), identifying 4 pi G rho as the source density.
Explains the Green's function idea for a general linear operator: solve with a delta-function source, then superpose against the actual source.
Since energy density and metric are both tensor fields, Newton's law should turn out to be just one component of the Einstein equation.

In electromagnetism and Newtonian gravity one fixes sources and solves for fields, but in GR the source tensor involves the metric being sought, forcing a simultaneous and difficult search for consistent g and T.
Defines the weak energy condition as a less strict alternative requiring only non-negative energy density for every observer.
Explains why the Ricci guess seemed reasonable (it keeps the volume-shrinking part of curvature) and dates it as Einstein's first suggestion in October 1915.
The contraction of the Bianchi identity relies on the sign changes of the lowered Riemann tensor under swaps within its first or second index pair.
Warns not to confuse the Einstein tensor with Newton's constant, both written G, and announces G = 1 units in later chapters.
Spells out the index raising and renaming that makes the divergence of the Einstein tensor vanish, and notes metric compatibility is used.
Reminds that a covariant derivative of a scalar field is just its partial derivative.

Physics recap in words for readers distracted by the algebra: Ricci captures volume-shrinking curvature but equating it to T violates conservation; the Bianchi identity built into the trace-reversed tensor restores it.
Notes that Example 13.4 temporarily restores factors of c to show the size of terms, and that R_00 is the sum over i of R^i_{0i0}.
Identifies the final equation as the one Einstein presented in November 1915 after rejecting his first attempt.
Points to Chapter 18 for a short history of cosmological solutions involving Lambda.

notable.summary: Demonstrate that Newton's second law together with the inverse-square gravitational law keep their form under Galilean boosts.
notable.why_notable: Highlights that Newtonian gravity is consistent with Galilean, not Lorentzian, relativity, sharpening why a new theory is needed.

notable.summary: Guided multi-part proof that the Laplacian of 1/r is -4 pi times a delta function: compute first and second derivatives of r and 1/r, show the Laplacian vanishes away from the origin, then use the flux of grad(1/r) through a surface enclosing the origin to obtain the weight -4 pi.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the identity quoted in Example 13.1, and the intermediate result (3 n^i n^j - delta^ij)/r^3 is the Newtonian tidal tensor that connects to Riemann components.

notable.summary: Check that contracting the Einstein tensor with the metric gives minus the Ricci scalar.
notable.why_notable: Justifies the name 'trace-reversed Ricci tensor' and rehearses the step used in Example 13.5.

difficulty.notes: The Newtonian half uses standard vector calculus and delta functions; the relativistic half is short but index-dense (Bianchi contractions, divergence of G) and quotes several results without proof (Bianchi identity, weak-field Riemann components). Conceptually the propose-and-refute structure is clear, but the physical meaning of the constant-trace contradiction, the nonlinearity loop, and the sign story for Lambda need unpacking. The margin physics recap helps novices. Minor printed issues: the geodesic deviation margin equation lacks the minus sign (as does GA eqn 11.38, though 11.6 and 11.39 have it), the letter G is overloaded three ways, and the Lambda sign explanation is loose.

Promise that gravity is a field theory of the metric obeying a differential equation involving curvature, fulfilled here.
Covariant derivative, semicolon notation, metric compatibility and the comma-to-semicolon rule used in the divergence arguments.

Ricci tensor and Ricci scalar definitions (eqns 13.6-13.7).
Geodesic deviation equation from which Riemann is extracted (margin eqn 13.4).
Energy-momentum tensor and its conservation law div T = 0, the constraint that drives the chapter.
Perfect-fluid energy-momentum components recalled in the closing heuristics.
Weak fields and the Newtonian limit revisited as the first triumph of the field equation.
Friedmann equations obtained by feeding a perfect fluid into the Einstein equation.
History of model universes with a cosmological constant (margin note 24).
Schwarzschild geometry, the vacuum solution R_{mu nu} = 0 of the equation derived here.
Einstein equation motivated from an action principle, a more systematic route than this chapter's plausibility argument.
