teaching_gems.gem: Put the natural wrong equation R^{mu nu} = kappa T^{mu nu} on the board, take its divergence, and let conservation plus the contracted Bianchi identity expose that it would force a uniform Universe; the Einstein tensor then appears as the fix.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners see why the odd-looking -g R/2 term is necessary instead of memorizing it, and they learn that conservation laws constrain which field equations are possible.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Field-equation workbench: learner picks coefficients in R_{mu nu} + a g_{mu nu} R + b g_{mu nu} = kappa T_{mu nu}; the app shows the divergence of the left side symbolically and, for a star-in-vacuum density map, the constraint it imposes on matter. Only a = -1/2 (any b) passes, and b is labelled as Lambda.

teaching_gems.gem: Rewrite Newton as a field theory until Poisson's equation reads 'two derivatives of a field proportional to its source', then transplant that shape into relativity with an unknown constant.
teaching_gems.why_effective: It gives a structural expectation (second-order equation for g sourced by T) before any tensor detail and reuses what learners already trust.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Morphing equation card: Laplacian Phi = 4 pi G rho animates term by term into G_{mu nu} = 8 pi G T_{mu nu}, with tooltips explaining what changed and why each change is forced.

teaching_gems.gem: Leave the constant kappa unknown until the end and determine it by requiring the 00 component to reproduce Poisson's equation.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows correspondence as a working tool that pins down numbers, and reveals that Newton sees only one component of a ten-component equation.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Kappa slider: learner varies kappa and the app computes the weak-field potential of the Earth or the Sun and the resulting orbital period of a test satellite, comparing with the Newtonian/observed value; the match occurs only at 8 pi G / c^4.

teaching_gems.gem: Contrast the one-way 'place sources, solve fields' workflow of electromagnetism with the source-geometry loop of GR (Fig. 13.2).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes nonlinearity concrete as a workflow difference rather than an abstract property, and explains why exact GR solutions are rare.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Iterative self-consistent star solver with a linear-mode toggle, animating each pass around the loop (see Fig. 13.2 redesign).

teaching_gems.gem: Trace the field equation to discover that the curvature scalar is set locally by the trace of the source, then trace-reverse to isolate Ricci.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A two-line manipulation yields a new, often more useful form and immediately shows that vacuum means Ricci-flat, not flat.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Source picker (dust, radiation, stiff fluid, vacuum energy): the app displays T_{mu nu}, its trace, R, and R_{mu nu} from version 2; radiation shows R = 0, vacuum energy shows R_{mu nu} proportional to g_{mu nu}.

teaching_gems.gem: Treat the cosmological constant as the leftover freedom of the consistency argument (anything with zero divergence can be added) and then relabel it as a vacuum energy-momentum tensor.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Lambda emerges from logic rather than from history or fudge, and moving it across the equals sign demonstrates that geometry and source terms are interchangeable bookkeeping.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Toggle Lambda on the left or right of the equation: the same term is displayed as geometry or as T^vac with rho and p = -rho, and a ball of test particles contracts or expands depending on the sign of rho + 3p.

teaching_gems.gem: Offer a words-only margin recap of the Bianchi argument for readers overwhelmed by indices.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Separates the logical skeleton (conservation must be built into geometry) from the algebra, letting learners of different levels follow the same argument.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Dual-track explanation toggle in the tutor: 'story mode' narrates the logic with icons; 'index mode' shows each contraction step, with synchronized highlighting.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive Poisson's equation from the integral law and recover the potential with a Green's function, then point out that superposition is what GR loses.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Sets up the contrast between linear and nonlinear field theories using a technique learners can actually compute.
teaching_gems.app_idea: 2D density painter: the potential is computed as a sum of -1/r kernels and the numerically evaluated Laplacian heat-map is shown to reproduce 4 pi G rho point by point.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Margin eqn 13.4 writes the geodesic deviation equation as D^2 xi / dtau^2 = +R(., u, xi, u). The minus sign is present in GA eqns 11.6 and 11.39 but missing from 11.38 as well, so the book is internally inconsistent on this sign.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Sign confusion about whether positive curvature focuses or defocuses neighbouring geodesics, and apparent inconsistency with Chapter 11.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use D^2 xi^a / dtau^2 = -R^a_{bcd} u^b xi^c u^d throughout and verify the sign with the Newtonian tidal tensor.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The explanation that positive Lambda repels 'owing to the difference in sign compared to positive T' is misleading: T^vac = -Lambda g / (8 pi G) has positive energy density and negative pressure p = -rho, and it satisfies the dominant energy condition; the repulsion comes from rho + 3p < 0.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may conclude that dark energy has negative energy density or violates the energy conditions just discussed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Compute T^vac_{tt} and T^vac_{ii} explicitly with signature (-,+,+,+), then show that the acceleration of a small ball of test particles is governed by rho + 3p.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The letter G stands for the Einstein tensor, Newton's constant and, in Example 13.2, a Green's function (eqn 13.22 even contains both G's in one expression). Only the first clash is flagged.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Misreading of equations such as Phi = G integral of G(x, x') rho, and of G = 8 pi G T.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: In the app use distinct glyphs: G_{mu nu} for Einstein, G_N for Newton's constant, and a script or subscripted symbol for the Green's function.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Margin note 11 defines the Green's function with L G = delta, but eqn 13.21 uses a 4 pi delta source, and the resulting kernel carries a minus sign and an external factor G.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Normalization and sign errors when learners try to apply the general recipe.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State one convention and show explicitly how the 4 pi and the minus sign are absorbed.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Uniqueness is not addressed: the authors admit the route is haphazard but do not mention that, in four dimensions, G_{mu nu} + Lambda g_{mu nu} is the only divergence-free symmetric tensor built from the metric and its first two derivatives (Lovelock's theorem).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may wonder whether other curvature combinations would work, or believe the plausibility argument is a proof.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a short note on the assumptions (locality, second order, divergence-free, four dimensions) and name Lovelock's theorem; point to the action-principle route in Chapter 40.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Energy-momentum conservation is described as encoded 'at least approximately' by div T = 0, and the chapter does not explain that the covariant law is exact but only local, with no local energy density for gravity.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion about whether energy is conserved in GR, and why gravitational energy is not part of T despite the nonlinearity discussion.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Clarify local versus global conservation, and note that the gravitational field's energy cannot be localized in a tensor.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 13.4 is terse: it recalls weak-field Gamma and Riemann components without derivation, silently drops Gamma-Gamma products and time derivatives, and uses the field equation itself (with vanishing spatial T) to set G^{ij} = 0.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The key identification R_00 = Laplacian Phi / c^2 may feel like magic, and the logic of using the equation to calibrate itself can seem circular.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show explicitly that R^i_{0j0} is the Newtonian tidal tensor to first order in Phi, and explain that the procedure is a consistency calibration valid to leading order.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Margin note 15 dates Einstein's Ricci-tensor proposal to October 1915; the proposal is usually associated with his 4 and 11 November 1915 Prussian Academy communications (and earlier notebook explorations of 1912-13).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor historical inaccuracy that a tutor might repeat.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'autumn 1915, in the weeks before the final November 25 paper' unless a precise source is checked.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The printed value of Newton's constant, 6.672(4)e-11, is an old determination.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Numerical answers differ slightly from modern references.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the CODATA value 6.67430(15)e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 in the app.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Margin note 10 says eqn 13.18 matches eqn 0.12, but the Overture's continuous-density Gauss law appears to be eqn 0.14, with 0.12 its point-mass form.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A learner following the pointer may find a slightly different equation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Cross-link both Overture equations when citing.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The chapter never states the vacuum consequence R_{mu nu} = 0 of version 2, nor that vacuum spacetime can still be curved.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The literal reading 'curvature = energy' suggests that empty space is flat, which would make Schwarzschild and gravitational waves puzzling.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Immediately after version 2, set T = 0, get Ricci-flatness, and contrast Ricci with the full Riemann tensor using the tidal field outside a star.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The contraction steps in Example 13.3 (which indices to raise, which symmetries turn Riemann into Ricci with a sign) are compressed into two lines.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Index-novices get lost and lose the thread of the conservation argument.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show each contraction with colour-coded indices and state the symmetry used at each step; offer the margin physics recap as a parallel track.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: In listing how Einstein's theory must differ from Newton's, the book cites Fermat's principle as saying light goes straight in flat spacetime, then cites starlight bending as proof that gravity warps spacetime. The inference is fast: Newtonian corpuscular light also bends (by half the GR amount), so bending alone does not force a geometric theory. The decisive evidence is the measured size of the deflection.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think any observed deflection of light rules out Newtonian gravity, or may mix up Fermat's least-time principle with a statement about straight lines.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say that Fermat's principle picks out paths of stationary travel time, which are straight only in flat geometry, and quote the 0.87 versus 1.75 arcsecond solar-limb values so the factor of 2 is what discriminates. Point ahead to the light-bending treatment in the Schwarzschild chapters.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'Newton says mass tells the potential how to curve via Poisson's equation. If gravity is geometry, what should play the role of the potential, and what the mass density?' Let the learner propose metric and energy-momentum before showing the template.

Recommended order: (1) Poisson as template, (2) recap Riemann -> Ricci -> R, (3) conservation of T, (4) the Ricci guess and why it fails, (5) Einstein tensor, (6) fixing kappa, (7) trace-reversed form and vacuum, (8) Lambda.

For learners weak on indices, run the Bianchi step in 'story mode' first: geometry has a built-in conservation law, matter has one too, and the field equation must make them agree. Show the index version only on request.

Check for understanding: ask why R^{mu nu} = kappa T^{mu nu} is not ruled out by dimensional analysis or rank but by conservation; a good answer mentions div T = 0 and the contracted Bianchi identity.
Check for understanding: ask the learner to compute the trace of G_{mu nu} (Exercise 13.3) and to explain why G is called trace-reversed.
Make the constant-trace contradiction concrete: inside a star the trace of T is roughly -rho, outside it is zero, so it cannot be constant everywhere.

When fixing kappa, emphasize that only the 00 component survives in the Newtonian regime and that pressure is negligible because p is roughly a few hundred thousand times smaller than rho c^2 even in the Sun's core (ratio about 2e-6).
Common learner question: 'If there is no matter, is spacetime flat?' Answer with version 2: Ricci vanishes, but Riemann (tidal curvature) need not; point ahead to Schwarzschild.

Common learner question: 'Why does a positive cosmological constant push things apart if it is positive energy?' Explain negative pressure and the rho + 3p rule rather than repeating the book's sign argument.

Common learner question: 'Is this derivation unique?' Say it is a plausibility argument; mention that under reasonable assumptions (four dimensions, second-order, divergence-free, built from the metric) only G + Lambda g works, and point to the action route in Chapter 40.
Watch the symbol G: always say 'Einstein tensor' or 'Newton's constant' aloud, and warn about the Green's function G in Example 13.2.

Use the heuristics list at the end of the chapter as a checklist before moving to Schwarzschild or cosmology problems: light cones, frame choice, index rules, general covariance, u . u = -1, perfect-fluid components.

Fixed a tutor note that said solar-core pressure is 'millions of times' smaller than rho c^2; the ratio is about 2e-6, i.e. a few hundred thousand.
Removed the 'diagram-driven' style tag: the chapter has only two small schematics, and its argument is carried by equations and Example boxes.
